sources: MacGregor, Alasdair Alpin. The Peat-Fire Flame: Folk-Tales and Traditions of the Highlands & Islands. Edinburgh: The Moray Press, 1937, 3.

text: Calamity meat is an Irish folkloric motif. The term named animals that died accidentally, such as by falling over a cliff or being crushed by a boulder. People buried the bodies whole. No one took a bite of them or cut a steak from their flanks. People thought fairies had put a spell on such animals. Some thought the body concealed an old dead fairy, left in place when fairies carried off the live animal. Before burial, farmers punctured the hide with an iron nail. This kept the soil free of later fairy power. Up to recent times country folk in Scotland and Ireland declined to eat the meat. They feared devouring a fairy cadaver.

okr.objective: Calamity meat names animals whose accidental deaths were blamed on fairies.
